RFK Jr Snaps at CNN's Dana Bash 'You're Sitting Here Attacking Me!' as Measles and Covid Clash Turns Explosive
A tense interview on CNN's 'State of the Union' highlights ongoing vaccine debates and public health concerns.
Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr pushed back sharply against CNN anchor Dana Bash on live television, telling her 'you've been sitting here attacking me' after she pressed him on his handling of America's worsening measles outbreak. The exchange, aired on 'State of the Union' on Sunday, 2 August 2026, lasted roughly 22 minutes and covered Covid-19 lockdowns, vaccine safety and autism research.
Kennedy, 72, repeatedly interrupted Bash and accused the media of 'press malpractice' during the pandemic. Bash, in turn, refused to let several of his claims go unchallenged, telling him at one point: 'I also don't want to use this interview to allow you to say things that aren't entirely true.'
A Heated Sunday Exchange
Kennedy's appearance came days after Dr Anthony Fauci invoked his Fifth Amendment rights more than 100 times during a congressional hearing into the pandemic response. Kennedy used the CNN platform to renew his criticism of Fauci, telling Bash it was 'absolute press malpractice' that journalists failed to scrutinise public health officials during Covid-19.
When Bash asked whether President Donald Trump, who was in office at the start of the pandemic, also bore some responsibility, Kennedy defended the president directly. 'President Trump, as you recall, wanted to end lockdowns,' he said. He argued that lockdowns had caused '3.5 million businesses' to close 'with no due process, no just compensation.'
Bash pressed him on preparation for a future public health crisis rather than constitutional rights. 'Forgive me, but you're just talking about rights, and I'm asking about a potential public health crisis that is coming,' she said. Kennedy fired back: 'Of course you do, because you were part of the problem!'
'You're Sitting Here Attacking Me'
The confrontation reached its sharpest point when Bash tried to redirect the conversation. 'Are you going to sit here and attack me, or do you want to have a conversation?' she asked. Kennedy replied instantly: 'You're attacking me.'
Bash rejected the characterisation outright. 'I'm not attacking you. I'm asking questions about how to prevent the next pandemic. That's what I'm trying to do,' she said. She added that she would not let him use CNN's airtime to make claims she considered false, including on Covid-19 vaccines.
Kennedy at one point accused her of behaving 'like a parrot' and told her she was 'talking nonsense,' insisting: 'You're making assertions you can't support.' CNN issued a statement defending its anchor after the broadcast. The network said Bash had asked 'tough, substantive questions' as 'the job of every journalist,' adding: 'We stand behind Dana, her reporting, and CNN's overall coverage of the Covid-19 pandemic.'
The Measles Figures Kennedy Faced
Much of the interview's tension stemmed from America's measles resurgence, now in its second consecutive record-breaking year. Bash told Kennedy that cases have reached their highest level in 35 years, with about 90 per cent occurring among people who are unvaccinated or whose vaccination status is unknown.
South Carolina has recorded more cases than any other state in 2026, driven largely by an outbreak in Spartanburg County that ran from October to April and became one of the largest in decades, with close to 1,000 cases.
Asked whether he bore any responsibility for the outbreak given his history as a vaccine sceptic, Kennedy answered: 'Absolutely not.' He pointed instead to higher measles rates in other countries. He argued the outbreak stemmed from pandemic-era lockdowns that kept children from receiving the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine on schedule.
Kennedy argued that lockdowns caused children to miss MMR doses, pointing to passages in Fauci's diaries as evidence – though he did not specify which passages or what they contained. Health officials recommend two doses of the MMR vaccine in childhood, which is around 97 per cent effective against infection.
Autism Claims Spark Further Confrontation
The interview grew more contentious when the conversation turned to autism. Bash noted that Trump had pressed Kennedy at a recent cabinet meeting on investigating a possible vaccine-autism link. She asked whether Kennedy had discussed with the president the 25 years of research finding none.
Kennedy replied that his department was 'doing all those things' and pointed to what he described as 73 studies linking acetaminophen use in late pregnancy to autism onset. While some observational studies have examined acetaminophen use in pregnancy, the research landscape is mixed and no causal link to autism has been established. Kennedy also did not name authors or mention study titles.
Bash countered directly on air. 'There have been more than 40 studies involving 5.6 million people to conclude there is no link between vaccines and autism,' she said, citing the head of the Committee on Infectious Diseases at the American Academy of Pediatrics.
The Secretary of Health accused Bash of rolling her eyes at him during the exchange, which she confirmed. Despite the friction, Kennedy did tell viewers directly that he supports parents vaccinating their children against measles.

*Wait. Was that a UFC fight or an interview? Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and CNN anchor Dana Bash turned Sunday’s edition of CNN’s “State of the Union” into a combative debate over COVID-19, vaccines, constitutional rights and the media’s role during the pandemic.
The nearly 20-minute interview intensified after Bash asked Kennedy how he would respond if the United States faced another public health emergency similar to COVID-19. Rather than focusing solely on pandemic preparedness, Kennedy said protecting Americans’ constitutional rights would be his first priority.
“I think one of the mistakes we made during COVID was suppressing constitutional rights,” Kennedy said, arguing that civil liberties should remain central during future health emergencies.
When Bash attempted to steer the discussion back toward public health, Kennedy shifted his criticism to the media.
“Because you were part of the problem,” he told Bash, accusing journalists of failing to aggressively question government officials and public health authorities during the pandemic.
Media, Vaccines and Public Trust Collide
Kennedy described much of the news media’s COVID-era reporting as “absolute press malpractice,” arguing that reporters accepted official guidance without sufficient scrutiny and discouraged meaningful debate over government policies.
Bash forcefully rejected that characterization and repeatedly challenged Kennedy’s statements about vaccines and public health, saying she would not allow claims she believed were unsupported by scientific evidence to go unchallenged.
As the conversation grew increasingly personal, Bash asked Kennedy whether he intended to continue attacking her or engage in a productive discussion.
“Do you want to sit here and attack me, or do you want to have conversations?” she asked.
“You’ve been sitting here and attacking me,” Kennedy replied.
At another point, Kennedy suggested Bash was misunderstanding aspects of the scientific discussion because she was “not a scientist,” prompting still more pushback as both repeatedly interrupted one another.
Measles and Autism Research Become Flashpoints
The interview later shifted to childhood vaccinations after Bash urged Kennedy to use his position as the nation’s top health official to encourage parents to vaccinate their children against measles amid ongoing outbreaks.
Following several minutes of debate, Kennedy looked directly into the camera and encouraged parents to have their children vaccinated against measles, even as he continued criticizing aspects of federal vaccine policy and pandemic-era decision-making.
The conversation then turned to autism, another issue that has long defined Kennedy’s public profile.
Kennedy argued additional research should continue examining possible links between vaccines and autism. Bash countered that the question has already been extensively studied and that current scientific research focuses largely on genetic and environmental factors associated with autism.
The disagreement highlighted one of the central controversies that has followed Kennedy throughout his public career and now accompanies his role as the nation’s top health official.
A Viral Political Moment
By the interview’s conclusion, Bash acknowledged the conversation had become unusually contentious while emphasizing that her responsibility was to provide viewers with accurate information grounded in established scientific evidence.
Kennedy maintained that journalists bear significant responsibility for failing to challenge public health officials more aggressively during the pandemic.
CNN later defended Bash’s handling of the interview, saying her questioning reflected the network’s commitment to factual reporting and scientific consensus on vaccine safety.
The exchange quickly generated widespread reaction across social media and political circles, with supporters praising Kennedy for confronting the media while critics applauded Bash’s persistent fact-checking and challenges to his claims.
Whether viewers sided with Kennedy or Bash, the interview underscored how debates over COVID-era policies, vaccines, media accountability and public trust continue to shape America’s political conversation years after the pandemic’s peak.
As Kennedy continues to lead the Department of Health and Human Services, those issues are likely to remain at the center of national debate.

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Sunday crashed out and hurled attacks at CNN host Dana Bash as she pressed him over his vaccine skepticism in a contentious 21-minute interview on “State of Union.”
During one heated moment, the conspiracy theorist questioned whether Bash could point to a study showing that children were protected by the COVID-19 vaccine and if it “did more harm than good.”
(Note: Millions of lives have been saved as a result of vaccination efforts, per some estimates, and a CDC report issued under President Donald Trump in December found that vaccinations against COVID-19 led to “substantially lower risks” for children during the prior respiratory virus season.)

“You are saying nonsense! You are saying something that you cannot show me a single study that says that,” Kennedy said.
“I am not saying nonsense,” Bash replied.
“You are talking —,” Kennedy began.
“Excuse me! Excuse me!” Bash interjected.
“Somebody told you —,” Kennedy chirped. “Cite me the study!”
“Let me — no, what studies are you talking about? You’re actually talking about studies that actually don’t exist,” responded Bash, who told Kennedy that the clash was “not productive.”
Earlier in the interview, Kennedy accused Bash of “absolute press malpractice” and being “part of the problem” in what he described as a dismantling of constitutional rights that occurred during the pandemic.
“Your job is a fierce skepticism toward authority and you weren’t doing that, you were beating up on people who were dissenting,” Kennedy declared.
“Do you want to sit here and attack me, or do you want to have conversations about public health?” Bash asked.
Later in the interview, Bash referred to Kennedy as “one of the leading voices questioning vaccine efficacy” and asked if he accepted “some responsibility” for the ongoing measles outbreak.
“Absolutely not,” said Kennedy, who made misleading claims about the safety and efficacy of the vaccine last year.
After Kennedy claimed he “never questioned the efficacy of the MMR vaccine (and later took Bash’s suggestion that he use the interview to call on parents to get their children vaccinated for measles), he promoted Trump’s unfounded claims linking use of Tylenol in pregnancies to autism.
“You’re rolling your eyes, Dana,” Kennedy remarked.
“I am, because I don’t want to have you use our air to say this,” she replied.

sources.text:
Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and “State of the Union” host Dana Bash clashed Sunday during an at-times-heated discussion of studies on vaccines and autism and the need to “trust the experts.”
During a Friday cabinet meeting, President Donald Trump pressed Kennedy about investigating whether certain vaccines are linked to the neurodevelopmental disorder — which impairs social interaction and can lead to focused interests and differences in sensory processing. Bash pressed Kennedy, claiming other studies had debunked claims that vaccines caused autism.
“Now, have you talked to [Trump] about medical research that have studied this for 25 years and found no link between autism and vaccines? And just that — this is my question here, because I don’t want to litigate that, my question is … because you are HHS secretary now — why not study what could cause autism, which scientists do believe starts with fetal brain development?” Bash asked. “Why not do some studies on that … — since you’re an environmental lawyer — whether there are environmental factors that go into contributing to a predisposed genetic situation?”
“We’re doing all those things. And that’s one of the ways that we found Tylenol,” Kennedy responded. “There’s 73 studies out that link Tylenol exposure during later pregnancy and during the perinatal period to autism onset. But you are wrong when you say that this issue has been studied. It has been studied. And you’re rolling your eyes, Dana, but this is another example—”
“I am, because I don’t want to have you use our air to say this,” Bash responded. “There have been more than 40 studies involving 5.6 million people to conclude there is no link between vaccines and autism. This is the head of the Committee of Infectious Diseases for the American Academy of Pediatrics.”

“And now let me tell you what the Institute of Medicine says— which is the National Academy of Sciences, which is the ultimate arbiter on vaccine safety in which it does not have an interest in this debate,” Kennedy said. “It says that none of the eight vaccines that are administered during the first six months of life have ever been studied for relationship to autism. It found two studies, one on the DTP [named to protect against three infectious diseases in humans: diphtheria (a bacterial infection), tetanus (lockjaw), and pertussis (whooping cough)] vaccine that show that it does cause autism, and one on the hepatitis B vaccine that again suggests that it does cause autism.”
“I’m not trying to link autism to anything,” Kennedy added.
“I am frustrated,” Bash later said. “The reason I’m frustrated is because I— you are the HHS secretary, and you are talking about things that lead to vaccine hesitancy in this country. And it is something that causes problems for people, when there is not anything—”
During Kenendy’s 22-minute appearance, he and Bash also clashed over the performance of Dr. Anthony Fauci — who took the Fifth over 100 times during a Senate hearing Wednesday — during which he compared Bash to a parrot.
“Let me ask you something,” Kennedy asked Bash. “Do you see your job as ending vaccine hesitancy, or do you see your job as telling the truth to the American people?”
“I see my job as telling the truth,” the host replied. “And the truth is that there is study after study after study. It’s one of the most studied things out there in science.”
“You’re repeating it like a parrot,” Kennedy said. “You’re repeating it like a parrot.”
“So are you,” said Bash.
“All you know how to do is repeat things that people told you and say, ‘Trust the experts,’” Kennedy soon responded. “Now we know that Anthony Fauci, who was the expert, was lying about everything, about masks, about the social distancing, about natural immunity, about the transmission from the vaccine, about the source of COVID. He was lying, and you were punishing people for not trusting the experts. And now you’re rolling out the experts again to talk about something that you have no personal knowledge of.”
“Well, guess what? That is my job to talk to people,” the host stated.
“Your job is to tell the truth to the American public and to maintain a posture of fierce skepticism toward government authority,” Kennedy replied.
“Am I allowed to talk?” Bash asked. “Yes, yes. And my job is to get as much information as I can.”
After Kennedy and Bash continued to clash over Fauci and COVID, Kennedy discussed efforts to address processed and “ultra-processed” foods, which was a priority of the Make America Healthy Again movement.
“I’m sorry that this turned into a very contentious conversation, and my job is to try to get the best information out there,” Bash said as the segment ended.
“Dana Bash is a veteran journalist who conducted a newsmaking interview with Secretary Kennedy in which he stated that he supports parents getting their children vaccinated against measles and addressed President Trump’s push for further study into autism and vaccines,” a CNN spokesperson told the Daily Caller News Foundation in a statement. “Asking tough, substantive questions to those in power is the job of every journalist, and Dana did hers incredibly well today.We stand behind Dana, her reporting, and CNN’s overall coverage of the COVID-19 pandemic.”
Kennedy did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the DCNF.

RFK Jr. pushes measles vaccine and blames Fauci's COVID-19 handling
HHS Secretary RFK Jr. slammed Anthony Fauci's diary and encouraged measles vaccines, in new contentious CNN interview.
Amid a record-breaking measles outbreak and days after former Chief Medical Advisor Dr. Anthony Fauci appeared before a Senate committee, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. encouraged Americans to get the MMR vaccine ahead of back-to-school season and blamed COVID-19 lockdowns for the measles cases.
On Sunday, Kennedy joined CNN for a conversation largely marked with personal attacks and scientific debate about studies which may or may not link vaccines to autism.
“You probably don't understand this because you're not a scientist,” Kennedy said to CNN's Dana Bash in a back-and-forth about the secretary's prior claims that vaccines are linked to autism.
"Well you're not either," Bash replied, noting the secretary's lack of a medical or scientific background.
Fauci and COVID-19
Kennedy said that the United States had the worst outcomes of any other country during the COVID-19 pandemic – a fact contested by Bash as not accurate. He blamed lockdowns for the damage and said that President Donald Trump wanted to reopen the country.
“In fact, in Anthony Fauci's diaries, he talks about how President Trump is calling him every day, trying to get him to reopen the country," Kennedy said.
On Wednesday, July 29, former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases Fauci testified – or rather pleaded the fifth – before a Senate committee that aimed to talk about the infectious disease expert's leadership during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Fauci did not answer questions, instead invoking his right against self-incrimination. Under fire was his diary, released days prior to the hearing by Sen. Rand Paul, in which Fauci called Trump "out of control," and lamented his own personal fame.
Kennedy also said that in addressing a future pandemic, "constitutional rights" must be the "number one priority." He slammed gain-of-function research – a method involving genetic alteration and regarded by many experts as useful in pandemic research, though controversial due to biosafety concerns – as not working. On Tuesday, July 28, the Trump administration announced plans to end the research.
The measles outbreak
Measles cases are at the highest level in 35 years, and Kennedy – a known vaccine critic – said parents should get their kids the MMR vaccine, which protects against measles, mumps and rubella.
“I never questioned the efficacy of the MMR vaccine,” Kennedy said.
He said he "absolutely" does not take responsibility for the rising numbers of cases when asked about his vaccine skepticism. Kennedy actually blamed rising rates on the COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns, citing Fauci's diary.
“In his diaries he says this is going to cause massive outbreaks of measles and more children, he says this, are going to die,” Kennedy said.
Fauci said in his diary that the group who "missed their measles vaccinations because of the shutdown" could lead to "far more excess deaths from measles among children than coronavirus deaths among children."
MAHA wins on processed foods
Kennedy is working on reforms for processed foods, a priority of his "Make America Healthy Again" agenda. He denied allegations that members of the administration are working to block his reforms due to lobbying from the food industry.
The secretary shared he is "confident" that in a month, both his changes to the ultra-processed food definition and "Generally Recognized as Safe" (GRAS) rule will be out to the public

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. got into a fiery clash with CNN host Dana Bash over the COVID-19 pandemic, vaccines and autism.
Tensions began to flare after Bash noted how the Kennedy scion has pinned a lot of the blame for the COVID-19 pandemic fallout on Dr. Anthony Fauci, who repeatedly pleaded the Fifth Amendment during questioning before a Senate panel last week.
But after Kennedy started describing his plan to respond to a future pandemic, the two really began taking the gloves off.
“We need to protect our constitutional rights. That is the primary obligation,” Kennedy said during CNN’s “State of the Union” on Sunday when asked about how he would deal with a pandemic in the future. “One of the mistakes we made in the last time was suppressing those rights so people weren’t being heard.”
Bash scoffed at his answer, saying that he was “talking about rights, and I’m asking about a potential public health crisis,” then attempted to move on to the next topic.
“Because you were part of the problem,” he fired back.
“It was absolute press malpractice … your job is furious skepticism of authority, and you weren’t doing that.”
The CNN anchor stressed that she didn’t want to let Kennedy get away with saying “things that are entirely untrue” and stressed that it is “factually true that the COVID vaccine worked.”
“Do you want to sit here and attack me, or do you want to have conversations?” Bashed vented.
An angry Kennedy fired back, “You’ve been sitting here and attacking me.”
Bash then attempted to pivot to the measles outbreak, but she quickly suggested that the COVID-19 vaccines worked, including on children.
Kennedy demanded she cite one study proving that to be true, and Bash claimed that there was research indicating that vaccine misinformation led to 100,000 to 200,000 more deaths in the US than what otherwise could’ve been.
“You are saying nonsense. You are saying something that you cannot [prove],” the HHS boss fumed
“I am not saying nonsense,” Bash interjected during some crosstalk. “Excuse me.”
Once they jumped into the measles discussion, Kennedy argued that it was an “international outbreak” and that the US is “doing better at handling it than any country in the world.”
The HHS boss also blamed the measles outbreak in the US on the COVID-19 pandemic and a segment of the population that refuses to get vaccinated due to religious reasons.
“What I want you to do is please use your bully pulpit to right now, as we’re getting close to back to school, say … to parents who have not vaccinated their kids that they should vaccinate their kids for measles because it is safe and it will help them save their children’s lives?” Bash said,
She pressed him to look into the camera and do that. Kennedy obliged.
Next, Bash grilled Kennedy on autism. He confirmed that President Trump “certainly does” want him to probe whether there are links between autism and vaccines.
“You are wrong when you say that this issue has been studied,” Kennedy said.
At one point, he said, “I know you’re flustered now.”
“Do you see your job as ending vaccine hesitancy or telling the truth to the American people?” he later added, before bashing her for repeating her lines “like a parrot.”
Bash decided to wrap up the interview on a somewhat conciliatory note after keeping him on for the full segment — in sharp contrast to other CNN anchors who have historically cut off guests that questioned them on air.
“I’m sorry that this turned into a very contentious conversation, and my job is to try to get the best information out there, and it concerns me when you come in and say things [that are wrong],” Bash concluded before ending the interview, which lasted over 20 minutes.

sources.news_title: RFK Jr. targets Fauci and pushes medical misinformation in fiery CNN interview
sources.text:
In attempting to rewrite the history of the US Covid-19 response, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Sunday pinned the blame for pandemic lockdowns on Dr. Anthony Fauci, while simultaneously reviving a string of debunked assertions about vaccines, RSV and measles.
Kennedy’s appearance came in the wake of a congressional hearing with Fauci last week, when the infections disease expert invoked his Fifth Amendment rights against self-incrimination more than 100 times, as Republicans lambasted him for his role in handling the pandemic.
Kennedy joined the chorus of criticism on CNN’s “State of the Union with Dana Bash,” saying President Donald Trump, who was in office at the beginning of the pandemic and notably downplayed the virus, was not to blame for the government’s response.
“Trump, as you recall, wanted to end the lockdowns. I think the thing that did the most damage to our country was the lockdowns,” he said.
The lockdowns were overseen by state and local leaders who were responding to ICUs being overwhelmed and hospitals asking for help to get control of the situation in the early stages of the pandemic.
Dr. Ashish Jha, who served as the White House Covid-19 response coordinator under President Joe Biden from 2022 to 2023, pushed back on Kennedy’s claims, saying, “accountability has to be with our political leaders,” while condemning his false claims on the inefficacy of vaccines.
“The accountability has to be with our political leaders, not with scientists who are giving advice. Second issue that i just want to quickly reflect on. There was a lot of information that Secretary Kennedy said that just isn’t true. It’s just factually not true,” Jha told Bash in an interview following Kennedy’s appearance.
The clash underscores a deepening division over public health authority at a critical juncture. As HHS secretary, Kennedy’s skepticism of mainstream science is no longer just outsider rhetoric; it now shapes official federal policy. His efforts to reframe the pandemic’s legacy come as the US battles its worst measles resurgence in more than three decades — a crisis experts warn is fueled directly by the type of vaccine misinformation and institutional distrust Kennedy amplified during the broadcast.
Measles
Kennedy pushed back on his handling of measles outbreaks in the US.
“The communities that are suffering from measles are almost all religious communities that just don’t vaccinate,” Kennedy told Bash.
A Mennonite community was one focus of an outbreak that began in West Texas last year. But the virus quickly spread among unvaccinated people outside that group, eventually reaching almost 800 cases — including the deaths of two children — before the outbreak was declared over.
There have been dozens more outbreaks in 2026, leading to the highest case count in 35 years, and more than 90% of them have been in people who aren’t vaccinated or whose vaccination status is unknown.
South Carolina has reported more measles cases in 2026 than any other state. An outbreak started raging across Spartanburg County in October; it would become the largest the US has seen in decades, with nearly 1,000 cases, before ending in April.
Health officials recommend two doses of the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine in childhood, and those two shots are 97% effective against measles infection.
But experts say the potential for measles outbreaks remains anywhere vaccination rates remain below 95%, a key immunity threshold for the highly contagious disease.
Pockets of low vaccination have been growing in recent years, which research attributes in no small part to misinformation.
Kennedy, who has frequently expressed skepticism about vaccines, told Bash that his agency’s websites recommend that “parents should get their children vaccinated for measles.”
“I’ve never questioned the efficacy of the MMR vaccine,” he said.
But in March 2025, as the outbreak in Texas spread to New Mexico and Oklahoma, he told Fox News’ Sean Hannity that measles outbreaks could be driven in part by people who have waning immunity from the vaccine.
“When you and I were kids, everybody got measles, and measles gave you … lifetime protection against measles infection. The vaccine doesn’t do that. The vaccine is effective for some people for life, but for many people, it wanes,” Kennedy told Hannity.
“Some years, we have hundreds of these outbreaks. … And, you know, part of that is that there are people who don’t vaccinate, but also the vaccine itself wanes,” he said.
RSV
Some of the criticism officials have leveled at Fauci concerns “gain-of-function research,” which involves the manipulation of a germ in a lab setting so researchers can study how it behaves as it evolves.
Kennedy claimed that gain-of-function research was responsible not just for the virus that causes Covid-19 but for other diseases, as well.
“The RSV epidemic that we have, that is the biggest killer of kids in this country today, came from these kind of experiments,” he said.
RSV, or respiratory syncytial virus, was first identified in the late 1950s in lab chimpanzees as well as in human children. What became known as gain-of-function research began two decades later, when scientists first figured out how to piece together genes from different organisms.
After 2011, when two teams of scientists modified the bird flu virus so it could become more dangerous and be transmitted between mammals through the air – something the virus hadn’t been able to do before — the US Department of Health and Human Services stepped in to create guidelines and mandate oversight of such research.
Acetaminophen and autism
Kennedy told Bash that dozens of studies link exposure to Tylenol during late pregnancy and the perinatal period to autism.
A 2025 review by US researchers of 46 earlier studies did suggest a possible link between prenatal exposure to acetaminophen — the drug found in Tylenol — and neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in children, but the researchers said the study does not prove the drug caused those conditions. They advised that pregnant women should continue to use acetaminophen as needed, at the lowest possible dose and for the shortest possible period.
Other research has found no sign of a link, including studies of millions of children followed for decades. However, there’s little research looking at autism prevalence relative to acetaminophen use during infancy or early childhood.
Major medical organizations support the use of acetaminophen to treat pain and fever during pregnancy, with recommendations reflecting that the benefits outweigh any potential risks.
Covid vaccines
Kennedy and Bash butted heads on whether Covid-19 vaccines had protected children, with the secretary asking her to cite research showing that the vaccine “did more good than harm.”
More than 700 million doses of Covid-19 vaccines have been administered in the US since they became available in late 2020, according to the World Health Organization. Researchers have estimated that the vaccines helped save 2.5 million lives around the world between 2020 and 2024.
The shots have been extensively tested and continually monitored for safety, and serious side effects such as anaphylaxis or myocarditis have happened but have been generally rare.
Research has also found that the vaccines are associated with lower risks of infection, hospitalization and complications in kids. In December, a report from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said that children who were vaccinated against Covid-19 in the previous respiratory virus season had a “substantially lower risk” of emergency department and urgent care visits related to the virus.
